appraisal_events.evidence: « elle m’avait ainsi menti en me jurant... qu’elle n’avait jamais eu avec l’amie de Mlle Vinteuil ces relations qu’au moment où Albertine me le jurait sa rougeur avait confessées » ; « Elle n’était plus qu’un nom, comme cette Mme de Charlus dont disaient avec indifférence : « Elle était délicieuse » ceux qui l’avaient connue » ; « Si la vie d’Albertine avait été vraiment coupable ».
appraisal_events.explanation: The narrator both convicts the dead Albertine of lying about her tastes — her blush treated as confession — and narrates her ontological erasure into a mere name, with her life kept under retrospective suspicion and investigation. The pitying tone (« Pauvre petite », her partial honesty) softens but does not reverse a dominant movement of exposure and effacement.

appraisal_events.evidence: « J’achetai combien de femmes qui ne m’apprirent rien » ; « je me mis à lire des livres sur les tables tournantes » ; « Avec la naïveté des théologiens antiques » ; « certaines folies douces de personnes qui par ailleurs semblent raisonnables » ; « ma santé, mon indécision, ma « procrastination », comme disait Saint-Loup ».
appraisal_events.explanation: The retrospective narrator diminishes his own past self, presenting his posthumous jealousy as futile and arbitrary, his consolations as absurd (« une telle supposition était absurde »), his beliefs as credulous, and his character as indecisive — a self-indictment reinforced by his admitted forgetting of his grandmother.

status_effects.explanation: She is narrated out of existence — reality closes over her, her trace is effaced, and she survives only as an indifferent name like Mme de Charlus.

Her word is retrospectively convicted of falsehood and her life is treated as presumptively « coupable » and worth investigating, though the narrator credits her with partial honesty and takes some blame himself.
He is locally at his weakest: grieving, jealous of a dead woman, buying women who teach him nothing, and sustaining a delusion that Albertine may walk back in.
The narration presents his credulity, arbitrary inquiry, and chronic « procrastination » — a label borrowed from Saint-Loup — as failings he himself concedes.

ambiguities: The passage stages blame for Albertine's concealment twice over: she lied and never went « jusqu'au bout de son aveu », yet the narrator twice concedes « c'était peut-être un peu ma faute » for having condemned such tastes too violently at Balbec. The text does not settle where the fault finally lands, so the diminishment of Albertine and the self-diminishment of the narrator are partly the same movement seen from two ends.

« cette Mme de Charlus » is not otherwise present in the local context and does not match the reference sheet's baron de Charlus; she is treated here as the baron's late wife, invoked only as an emblem of posthumous reduction to a name, so her identification is left unresolved.
